conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: StopBeyondSignalBarInitialStop
candidates.quote: A reasonable location for a protective stop is at one tick above the high of the signal bar.
candidates.description: The initial protective stop for a stop-entry trade is placed stopTicks beyond the signal bar's extreme opposite the trade direction: for a long entry, stopTicks below the low of the signal bar (the bar whose breach triggered the entry, i.e. the bar immediately before the entry bar). Held until either the entry-bar tightening rule (R27-02) fires or the market moves strongly in the trade's favor.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop order one tick beyond the signal bar's extreme

complexity.reason: needs BarsSinceEntry to locate the signal bar relative to the current bar and hold that price across bars until it is replaced

notes: Brooks's own example is a short (sell stop below the prior bar's low); the long side is the mirror as required by the pseudocode convention.

candidates.name: TightenStopAfterStrongEntryBar
candidates.quote: After the entry bar closes, if it has a strong bear body, tighten the stop to one tick above the entry bar. Otherwise, keep the stop above the signal bar until after the market begins to move strongly in your direction.
candidates.description: Once the entry bar closes, if it closed with a strong body in the trade's direction, replace the wider signal-bar stop (R27-01) with a tighter stop stopTicks beyond the entry bar's own extreme; otherwise keep the original signal-bar stop.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop order, tightened to one tick beyond the entry bar

complexity.reason: needs BarsSinceEntry to fire exactly once after the entry bar closes, a strong-bar body test, and persistent stop-price state across the trade

notes: The strong-body test reuses the same shape as the trend-bar-body-fraction primitive used elsewhere in the corpus (e.g. rules/TrendBarBodyFraction-style pseudocode).

candidates.name: FixedTickScalpTargetWithFillSlippage
candidates.quote: It usually takes a six-tick move beyond the signal bar to net a four-tick scalp and a ten-tick move to make an eight-tick scalp in the Eminis.
candidates.description: A fixed-tick profit-target exit at scalpTicks beyond the entry price, but modeled with the realistic assumption that a resting limit order needs the market to trade fillSlippageTicks beyond the target price to actually fill (so the observed move needed beyond the signal bar is entryOffsetTicks + scalpTicks + fillSlippageTicks).
candidates.pseudocode:
targetPrice = ctx.EntryPrice() + scalpTicks * tickSize;
exitLongAtTarget = high[0] >= (targetPrice + fillSlippageTicks * tickSize);
candidates.book_order_type: limit order to take profit, offset by an extra tick to model realistic fills

complexity.reason: single arithmetic comparison against the entry price plus fixed tick offsets

notes: TakeProfit in the catalog is dollar-based off open profit; this is the tick/price-based form Brooks describes, with the extra fill-slippage tick as a distinguishing feature.
The six-tick / ten-tick examples are just entryOffsetTicks(1) + scalpTicks(4 or 8) + fillSlippageTicks(1); recorded as one parameterized rule rather than two.

rejected.quote: This is the single most reliable entry approach, and beginners should restrict themselves to it until they become consistently profitable.
rejected.reason: a skill-level recommendation for which order type to use, not a bar-level trading condition

chapter_summary: A short, mechanical chapter on the mechanics of stop entries: naming the signal bar and entry bar, placing the initial protective stop one tick beyond the signal bar, tightening it to one tick beyond the entry bar once it closes with a strong body, and the tick arithmetic showing that a limit profit target needs an extra tick of overshoot to fill (six ticks beyond the signal bar to net a four-tick scalp, ten ticks to net eight). No new pattern-recognition primitives; all three candidates are Exit-side stop/target mechanics that likely overlap with the corpus's existing dollar-based Stop/TakeProfit family once authored in price terms instead of dollars.
